addmaths-0606-logs-bases-and-powers.description: Convert between powers and logarithms. Use positive arguments, including fractional and negative powers.

sections.title: What does a logarithm return?
sections.label: Inverse powers
sections.intro: Read a log statement as a question about an exponent. For a legal base, each positive argument has one corresponding power.

blocks.html: The statements \(b^u=v\) and \(\log_{b}\left(v\right)=u\) have the same meaning when \(b>0,\ b\ne1,\ v>0\).

figure.alt: Increasing exponential and logarithmic curves reflected about the diagonal.
figure.caption: The two shapes exchange input and output across \(y=x\). The marked points are exchanged too.

blocks.prompt:
A scale uses the base \(25\).

Give the exact value of \(\log_{25}\left(125\right)\).
blocks.hint: Express the base and the argument as powers of the same number.
blocks.solution:
Write the base and argument as powers of \(5\).

If the logarithm is \(x\), then \(5^{(2)x}=5^{3}\). Match exponents.

\(\frac{3}{2}\)

retry.feedback: The exponent of the displayed argument is relative to the smaller base. Divide by the exponent used to form the stated base.

blocks.html: The logarithm is the exponent. Keep the base and the argument in their own roles.

blocks.prompt: Find the exact value of \(\log_8\!\left(\frac12\right)\).
blocks.hint: Write \(\frac12\) as a power of \(2\).
blocks.solution:
Let \(u\) be the required logarithm. Then \(8^u=\frac12\), or \(2^{3u}=2^{-1}\).

Equal exponents give \(3u=-1\), hence \(u=-\frac13\).

retry.feedback: \(\frac12\) is below \(1\), so a base above \(1\) needs a negative exponent.

blocks.html: Try to rewrite the base and argument as powers of one smaller base.

sections.title: Can the base be the unknown?
sections.label: Unknown base
sections.intro: Turn a logarithmic equation into an exponential equation. Undo the stated exponent to recover the base.

blocks.html: For unknown positive \(b\), \(\log_{b}\left(v\right)=u\) gives \(b=v^{1/u}\) if \(u\ne0\) and the answer is a legal base.

blocks.prompt: Find the positive base \(b\) in \(\log_b\!\left(64\right)=2\).
blocks.hint: Write \(b^{2}=64\) first, then isolate the base.
blocks.solution: \(b^2=64\), which gives \(b=\pm8\) algebraically. A logarithm requires \(b>0\), so \(b=8\).

retry.feedback: The negative algebraic candidate is an invalid logarithm base.

blocks.html: Multiplying by a fractional exponent is different from raising to that exponent.

blocks.prompt: Find the positive base \(b\) in \(\log_b\!\left(16\right)=-2\).
blocks.hint: Write \(b^{-2}=16\) first, then isolate the base.
blocks.solution: \(b^{-2}=16\), so \(b^2=\frac{1}{16}\). The positive square root is \(b=\frac14\).

retry.feedback: The exponent is negative. Take the reciprocal to obtain \(b^2\) before taking its root.

blocks.html: Check the recovered base is positive and different from one.

sections.title: Which arguments are allowed?
sections.label: Domain
sections.intro: A positive real base raised to any real power always gives a positive result. The inverse logarithm therefore needs its argument to be positive.

blocks.html: For a logarithm of a whole expression, require that whole expression to be greater than zero, for example \(\lg(5x-1)\) needs \(x>\tfrac15\).

blocks.prompt:
Let \(g(x)=\log_{7}\left(2x+3\right)\) on its natural domain.

State the domain of \(g\), in interval notation or as an inequality.
blocks.hint: Solve the inequality that requires the logarithm argument to be positive.
blocks.solution:
The argument must be strictly positive: \(2x+3>0\).

The coefficient of \(x\) is positive. Divide without reversing the inequality.

\(x>-\frac{3}{2}\)

retry.feedback: The argument would be zero at the lower endpoint. A logarithm of zero is undefined.

blocks.html: The boundary itself is excluded because the argument is zero there.

blocks.prompt: State the natural domain of \(g(x)=\log_3(7-x)\).
blocks.hint: Set the whole argument greater than zero and solve the inequality.
blocks.solution: The argument must be positive. \(7-x>0\Longleftrightarrow x<7\). The endpoint gives zero and is excluded.

retry.feedback: The logarithm of zero is undefined. The boundary needs an open bracket.

blocks.html: Solve the argument inequality before solving the log equation.

examples.title: Read a fractional power
examples.question: Evaluate \(\log_4 8\) exactly.
solution: Let \(u=\log_4 8\). The logarithm asks for the power \(u\) such that \(4^u=8\).
Write both numbers in base \(2\): \((2^2)^u=2^3\), so \(2^{2u}=2^3\). Equal powers of \(2\) have equal exponents.

examples.title: Recognise a negative power
examples.question: Evaluate \(\log_{27}\!\left(\frac19\right)\) exactly.
solution: The argument is below \(1\), while the base is above \(1\). The exponent must be negative.
\(u=-\frac23\). Taking a cube root of \(27\) and then the reciprocal of its square gives \(\frac19\).

examples.title: Choose the legal square root
examples.question: Find \(b\) if \(\log_b 49=2\). Explain why only one base works.
solution: Write \(b^2=49\). The algebraic candidates are \(b=7\) and \(b=-7\).
A real logarithm requires a positive base other than \(1\). This leaves \(b=7\).
Check: the exponent that takes \(7\) to \(49\) is \(2\).

examples.title: Recover a base below one
examples.question: Find \(b\) if \(\log_b 8=-3\).
solution: Rewrite the equation as \(b^{-3}=8\). Reciprocate both sides to get \(b^3=\frac18\).
The positive cube root is \(b=\frac12\), which is a legal base.
Check: \(\left(\frac12\right)^{-3}=2^3=8\).

examples.title: Find the allowed inputs first
examples.question: For \(g(x)=\log_5(2x+1)\), state the domain and solve \(g(x)=1\).
solution: The entire argument must be positive: \(2x+1>0\), so \(x>-\frac12\).
The target log value is \(1\), so \(2x+1=5\). Subtracting \(1\) gives \(2x=4\), hence \(x=2\).
The input \(2\) is in the domain and \(g(2)=\log_5 5=1\).

examples.title: Reverse the boundary inequality
examples.question: State the domain of \(h(x)=\log_2(5-2x)\). Then solve \(h(x)=0\).
solution: For the argument to be positive, \(5-2x>0\). Adding \(2x\) to both sides gives \(5>2x\), so \(x<\frac52\).
At log value zero the argument is \(2^0=1\). Thus \(5-2x=1\), so \(2x=4\) and \(x=2\).
The boundary \(x=\frac52\) gives argument zero. The root \(x=2\) gives argument one, so it is allowed.

addmaths-0606-logs-log-laws.description: Use the product, quotient and power laws to combine and evaluate logarithms.

sections.title: Why does subtraction divide the arguments?
sections.label: Quotient law
sections.intro: Dividing powers of the same number subtracts their exponents. Logarithms return those exponents.

blocks.html: With positive arguments \(A,B\), \(\log_{b}\left(A\right)-\log_{b}\left(B\right)=\log_{b}\left(\tfrac{A}{B}\right)\).

blocks.prompt:
Consider \(L=\log_{4}\left(2048\right)-\log_{4}\left(8\right)\).

Evaluate L exactly.
blocks.hint: Divide the two positive arguments before evaluating the logarithm.
blocks.solution:
The difference of logs has argument \(\frac{2048}{8}=256\).

Since \(4^{4}=256\), the logarithm is \(4\).

\(4\)

blocks.html: Subtracting the arguments gives a different number. Form the quotient first.

blocks.prompt: Evaluate \(\log_3 2-\log_3 18\) exactly.
blocks.hint: The second argument goes in the denominator of the quotient.
blocks.solution:
Both arguments are positive and the bases agree, so combine the logs as \(\log_3\!\left(\frac{1}{9}\right)\).

The quotient is \(3^{-2}\). The logarithm is \(-2\).

retry.feedback: The second logarithm is the one subtracted. Keep the first argument in the numerator.

blocks.html: Keep the order of arguments: the subtracted log supplies the denominator.

sections.title: How can I write several terms as one log?
sections.label: Power product
sections.intro: First move an outside coefficient to a power of the argument. Then join same-base logs by multiplying or dividing arguments.

blocks.html: Use \(n\log_{b}\left(x\right)=\log_{b}\left(x^n\right)\) before applying the product and quotient laws. Each original argument must be positive.

blocks.prompt: For \(x>0\), write \(2\log_5 x+\log_5 6-\log_5 2\) as a single logarithm.
blocks.hint: Move any coefficient into the exponent of its argument before combining terms.
blocks.solution:
The combined argument is \(\frac{6x^2}{2}=3x^2\).

The result is \(\log_5\!\left(3x^2\right)\).

retry.feedback: Move the coefficient of the log into the exponent before the multiplication.

blocks.html: No log law replaces a logarithm of a sum by a sum of logarithms.

blocks.prompt: For \(x>0\), write \(\log_7(2x)+\log_7 3-\log_7(x^2)\) as a single logarithm.
blocks.hint: Move any coefficient into the exponent of its argument before combining terms.
blocks.solution:
The combined argument is \(\frac{(2x)(3)}{x^2}=\frac6x\).

The result is \(\log_7\!\left(\frac6x\right)\).

retry.feedback: Divide by the argument of the term being subtracted.

blocks.html: For symbolic arguments, write the combined argument clearly before simplifying it.

sections.title: Can I evaluate the logs before using a law?
sections.label: Integer powers
sections.intro: When an argument is a familiar power of the base, you can evaluate the log directly and then do the arithmetic.

blocks.html: If \(A=b^u\) and \(B=b^v\), then \(k\log_{b}\left(A\right)-\log_{b}\left(B\right)=ku-v\).

blocks.prompt:
The value \(D\) is defined by \(D=3\log_{3}\left(9\right)-\log_{3}\left(81\right)\).

Evaluate D exactly.
blocks.hint: Evaluate each logarithm as an exponent before applying the outside coefficient.
blocks.solution:
The individual logarithms are \(2\) and \(4\).

Substitute into the expression to get \(3\times2-4=2\).

\(2\)

retry.feedback: The coefficient multiplies the entire first logarithm.

blocks.html: The coefficient multiplies the value of its own logarithm. It does not multiply the log base.

blocks.prompt: Evaluate \(\log_5 25-\log_5 125\) without a calculator.
blocks.hint: Identify the powers of the base that give the two arguments.
blocks.solution: The two logarithms are \(2\) and \(3\). Therefore the value is \(2-3=-1\).

retry.feedback: Take the first exponent minus the second. Swapping them changes the sign.

blocks.html: Check your evaluation by combining the logs and simplifying the powers inside.

examples.title: Divide the arguments first
examples.question: Evaluate \(\log_3 54-\log_3 2\) exactly.
solution: Both arguments are positive and both logarithms have base \(3\). Apply the quotient law.
Since \(3^3=27\), the exact value is \(3\).

examples.title: Keep the quotient in order
examples.question: Evaluate \(\log_2 3-\log_2 24\) without a calculator.
solution: The subtracted log gives the denominator: \(\log_2\!\left(\frac{3}{24}\right)=\log_2\!\left(\frac18\right)\).
As \(\frac18=2^{-3}\), the value is \(-3\).
The value is negative because the quotient is below \(1\) and the base is above \(1\).

examples.title: Combine a power, a product and a quotient
examples.question: For \(x>0\), write \(2\log_3 x+\log_3 6-\log_3 2\) as one logarithm. Then solve when its value is \(3\).
solution: Apply the power law to the first term, producing \(\log_3(x^2)\). The product and quotient laws then give \(\log_3\!\left(\frac{6x^2}{2}\right)=\log_3(3x^2)\).
An output of \(3\) means \(3x^2=3^3=27\). Divide by \(3\) to get \(x^2=9\).
The original condition \(x>0\) leaves \(x=3\).

examples.title: Simplify the argument while preserving the domain
examples.question: Write \(\log_5(2x)+\log_5 5-\log_5(x^2)\) as one logarithm, with its original domain.
solution: The term \(\log_5(2x)\) requires \(x>0\). This already ensures \(x^2>0\).
Combine the terms as \(\log_5\!\left(\frac{10x}{x^2}\right)\). On the original domain \(x\) is non-zero, so cancel one factor of \(x\).
The result is \(\log_5\!\left(\frac{10}{x}\right)\), for \(x>0\).

examples.title: Evaluate familiar powers directly
examples.question: Find \(D=2\log_4 16-\log_4 64\), and then find \(4^D\).
solution: Because \(16=4^2\) and \(64=4^3\), the two logarithms are \(2\) and \(3\).
\(D=2\cdot2-3=1\). The coefficient \(2\) affects the first logarithm only.
Substituting the result in the exponent gives \(4^D=4\).

examples.title: Use a fractional power accurately
examples.question: Find \(D=\log_9 3-2\log_9 27\), and then find \(9^D\).
solution: Write \(3=9^{1/2}\) and \(27=(3)^3=9^{3/2}\). The log terms have values \(\frac12\) and \(\frac32\).
\(D=\frac12-2\cdot\frac32=-\frac52\).
\(9^D=3^{-5}=\frac{1}{243}\). The negative exponent gives a reciprocal.

sections.title: How do I choose a better base?
sections.label: Same base
sections.intro: Turn the log into an exponential equation, take logs in a new base, then solve for the original exponent. A base shared by both numbers can give an exact rational result.

blocks.prompt: Use a common base to find the exact value of \(\log_{16}\!\left(8\right)\).

The change-of-base ratio is \(\frac{3}{4}\).

sections.title: What does the reciprocal of a logarithm mean?
sections.label: Reciprocal
sections.intro: If you swap which value is the log base and which is the argument, all the terms in the base-change ratio swap.

blocks.html: When \(a,b>0\) and both differ from 1, \(\frac{1}{\log_{a}\left(b\right)}=\log_{b}\left(a\right)\).

blocks.prompt:
Here a reciprocal means the number 1 divided by the logarithm. Let \(R=\frac{1}{\log_{9}\left(27\right)}\).

blocks.hint: Find the base-change ratio, then invert the fraction.

The inner log is \(\frac{3}{2}\) because \(9\) and \(27\) are powers of \(3\).

Invert this value, or interchange the base and the argument using change of base.

\(\frac{2}{3}\)

retry.feedback: This is the logarithm itself. The displayed expression is its reciprocal.

blocks.html: A reciprocal is a fraction with numerator 1. It is different from an inverse function.

blocks.prompt: Evaluate \(\frac{1}{\log_8 4}\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Swap the base and argument, or find the inner log before taking its reciprocal.
blocks.solution:

Its reciprocal is \(\frac32\).

examples.title: Choose a small common base
examples.question: Use a change of base to find \(\log_{16}8\) exactly.
solution: Both numbers are powers of \(2\). Use base \(2\) in both positions of the ratio.
\(\log_{16}8=\frac{\log_2 8}{\log_2 16}=\frac34\). The original base \(16\) supplies the denominator.

examples.title: Change base when the argument is below one
examples.question: Find \(\log_8\!\left(\frac14\right)\) exactly.
solution: Use base \(2\) because \(8=2^3\) and \(\frac14=2^{-2}\).
The denominator is positive and the numerator is negative, so the sign is consistent with the argument.

examples.title: Use a given logarithm in the numerator
examples.question: For positive \(a,b\), \(\lg a=3\) and \(\lg b=2\). Calculate \(\log_b(a^3)\) without writing either \(a\) or \(b\) as a number.
solution: Change the base to \(10\): \(\log_b(a^3)=\frac{\lg(a^3)}{\lg b}\).
The numerator is \(3\lg a=9\) and the denominator is \(2\). The result is \(\frac92\).
Using the logarithms directly avoids constructing the much larger number \(a^3\).

examples.title: Handle a quotient before substituting
examples.question: For positive \(a,b\), \(\lg a=2\) and \(\lg b=5\). Find \(\log_a\!\left(\frac{b}{a^2}\right)\) exactly.
solution: After changing to base \(10\), use the quotient and power laws in the numerator.
\(\log_a\!\left(\frac{b}{a^2}\right)=\frac{\lg b-2\lg a}{\lg a}=\frac{5-4}{2}=\frac12\).
The result is positive because \(\lg(b/a^2)=1\), so \(b/a^2>1\).

examples.title: Swap the argument and base to take a reciprocal
examples.question: Evaluate \(\frac{1}{\log_9 3}\) and state why the reciprocal exists.
solution: The inner log is \(\frac12\) since \(9^{1/2}=3\). It is non-zero, so its reciprocal is defined.
\(\frac{1}{\log_9 3}=2\). Using the reciprocal identity gives the same result: \(\log_3 9=2\).

examples.title: Change base to telescope a product
examples.question: Simplify \(\log_2 5 \cdot \log_5 8\) exactly.
solution: Change the second log to base \(2\): \(\log_5 8=\frac{\log_2 8}{\log_2 5}\).
Now the product is \(\log_2 5\cdot\frac{\log_2 8}{\log_2 5}=\log_2 8\), since \(\log_2 5\ne0\).
\(8=2^3\), so the product equals \(3\).

addmaths-0606-logs-log-equations.description: Check domains first, solve a combined equation and test every candidate in the original logarithms.

sections.title: How do I start with one logarithm?
sections.label: Single log
sections.intro: State the restriction first. Convert the log equality into exponential form. Then solve the simpler algebraic equation and check the original argument.

blocks.html: Use \(\log_{a}\left(U\right)=r\) to obtain \(U=a^r\). The function requires \(U>0\).

blocks.prompt:
Consider \(\log_{2}\left(7x-3\right)=4\).

Find the exact solution.
blocks.hint: Rewrite in exponential form and solve the resulting linear equation.
blocks.solution:
Rewrite the equation as \(7x-3=16\).

Add \(3\) and divide by \(7\). The argument is \(16\), so it is positive.

\(x=\frac{19}{7}\)

retry.feedback: The linear expression subtracts the constant. Add that constant to both sides before dividing.

blocks.html: The right-hand side of the new equation is a power of the log base.

blocks.prompt: Solve \(\log_2(x+3)=3\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Rewrite the equation as a power of 2 before isolating the input.
blocks.solution:
The argument needs \(x>-3\). The power form is \(x+3=2^3=8\), so \(x=5\).

The argument is positive at this solution.

blocks.html: Show the original domain even when you expect only one candidate.

sections.title: Which root of the product equation is valid?
sections.label: Products roots
sections.intro: Combine same-base logarithms into one. The resulting product can be positive even when both individual arguments are negative.

blocks.html: A solution must make each original argument positive. The condition \(UV>0\) alone is weaker than \(U>0\) and \(V>0\) together.

blocks.prompt: Solve \(\log_3(x-1)+\log_3(x+1)=1\) over the reals. Give the valid solution.
blocks.hint: Find the domain from the two original arguments before factorising.
blocks.solution:
Both log arguments need to be positive, so \(x>1\).

Combine the logs and write in power form: \((x-1)(x+1)=3^1=3\).

Expand and collect terms to get \(x^2-4=0\). Factorise as \((x-2)(x+2)=0\). Only \(x=2\) is in the original domain.

retry.feedback: This root makes an original argument non-positive. Recheck the two conditions before choosing the solution.

blocks.html: Do not accept a quadratic root without testing the original arguments.

blocks.prompt:
Solve \(\log_{2}\left(x-13\right)+\log_{2}\left(x-12\right)=1\) over the reals.

Give the valid solution.
blocks.hint: Combine the logarithms as a product and solve the quadratic.
blocks.solution:
Both arguments must be positive. The stronger restriction is \(x>13\).

Combine the logs and solve \((x-13)(x-12)=2\).

The candidates are \(14\) and \(11\). Only \(14\) satisfies the restriction.

\(x=14\)

retry.feedback: That root solves the product equation, but the individual log arguments are not positive.

blocks.html: Write a rejection reason beside any candidate you exclude.

sections.title: How can I handle subtraction or different bases?
sections.label: Quotients bases
sections.intro: A difference of same-base logs gives a quotient. If the bases differ, change to a common base before combining any terms.

blocks.html: Set the quotient of the original arguments to \(a^r\) when their log difference in base \(a\) equals \(r\). Check that the denominator is positive.

blocks.prompt:
Consider \(\log_{4}\left(19x-22\right)-\log_{4}\left(x-1\right)=2\).

Find the exact value of x.
blocks.hint: Use the quotient law and solve the resulting linear equation.
blocks.solution:
The original arguments require \(x>\frac{22}{19}\) and \(x>1\).

Combine to a quotient and rearrange to \(19x-22=16(x-1)\).

Collect like terms. At \(2\), the arguments are \(16\) and \(1\), so the value is valid.

\(2\)

blocks.html: Cross-multiplying before noting the domain can introduce candidates excluded by an original argument.

blocks.prompt: Solve \(\log_2(x+3)-\log_2(x-1)=1\) exactly.
blocks.hint: The subtraction becomes a quotient. Check where both arguments are positive.
blocks.solution:
The original domain requires \(x>1\).

The quotient equation gives \(x+3=2(x-1)\).

Collecting like terms gives \(x=5\), so \(x=5\), which satisfies the domain.

blocks.html: At the end, substitute to confirm that both log arguments are positive.

examples.title: Solve one log equation with a positive exponent
examples.question: Solve \(\log_3(2x-1)=2\). Show the restriction on \(x\).
solution: The original argument requires \(2x-1>0\), so \(x>\frac12\).
In exponential form \(2x-1=3^2=9\). Add \(1\), then divide by \(2\), giving \(x=5\).
This satisfies the restriction and gives the original log value \(\log_3 9=2\).

examples.title: Use the reciprocal for a negative exponent
examples.question: Solve \(\log_2(3-x)=-2\) exactly.
solution: The argument is positive when \(x<3\). The equivalent equation is \(3-x=2^{-2}=\frac14\).
Add \(x\) and subtract \(\frac14\): \(x=3-\frac14=\frac{11}{4}\).
\(\frac{11}{4}<3\), and substituting gives a positive argument \(\frac14\).

examples.title: Reject the root that gives negative arguments
examples.question: Solve \(\log_2(x-1)+\log_2(x+1)=3\) over the reals.
solution: Both arguments must be positive. The intersection of \(x>1\) and \(x>-1\) is \(x>1\).
Combine the logs and write the result as a power: \((x-1)(x+1)=2^3=8\). Then \(x^2-1=8\) and \(x^2=9\).
The candidates are \(3\) and \(-3\). The second violates \(x>1\), so \(x=3\) only. The two positive arguments at \(3\) are \(2\) and \(4\), whose product is \(8\).

examples.title: Use an interval restriction from two logs
examples.question: Solve \(\log_2(x-1)+\log_2(5-x)=\log_2 3\).
solution: For both original logs to exist, \(x-1>0\) and \(5-x>0\), so \(1<x<5\).
Combine the left-hand logs. Equal logs in base \(2\) have equal arguments, giving \((x-1)(5-x)=3\).
Expanding gives \(-x^2+6x-5=3\). Therefore \(x^2-6x+8=(x-2)(x-4)=0\).
Both \(2\) and \(4\) lie inside \((1,5)\), so both solutions are valid.

examples.title: Solve a quotient equation
examples.question: Solve \(\log_2(x+3)-\log_2(x-1)=1\).
solution: The original arguments both need to be positive, so \(x>1\). Take the quotient in the written order.
Multiply by \(x-1\), which is positive on the domain. Then \(x+3=2x-2\), giving \(x=5\).
At \(x=5\) the quotient is \(\frac84=2\) and both logs exist.

examples.title: Bring different logarithms to one base
examples.question: Solve \(\log_2 x+\log_4(2x)=2\) exactly.
solution: The original arguments require \(x>0\). Let \(u=\log_2 x\). Because \(\log_2 4=2\), the change-of-base formula gives \(\log_4(2x)=\frac{\log_2 2+\log_2 x}{2}=\frac{1+u}{2}\).
The equation becomes \(u+\frac{1+u}{2}=2\). Multiplying by \(2\) gives \(2u+1+u=4\), so \(u=1\).
Return to \(x\): \(\log_2 x=1\) gives \(x=2\). The original two terms are \(1\) and \(1\).

sections.title: When can I match the exponents?
sections.label: Matching bases
sections.intro: Look for a small common base before taking any logarithms. Since legal exponential functions pass each positive value once, equal outputs give equal exponents.

blocks.html: If \(b>0\) and \(b\ne1\), then \(b^u=b^v\) implies \(u=v\).

blocks.prompt: Solve \(8^{x+1}=4^{2x-1}\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Write both bases as powers of \(2\).
blocks.solution:
The two exponents in base \(2\) are \(3(x+1)\) and \(2(2x-1)\). Equate them.

Collecting terms gives \(-x=-5\), so \(x=5\).

blocks.html: When changing the base of a power, multiply the entire exponent by the extra power.

blocks.prompt:

blocks.html: State the common base in your working, then solve a linear equation if possible.

sections.title: What if the bases do not match?

sections.intro: Isolate the term with the unknown exponent. Take logarithms of both sides so the power law makes that exponent a multiplier.

blocks.html: For \(a>0\), \(a\ne1\) and \(b>0\), the solution of \(a^x=b\) is \(x=\frac{\ln b}{\ln a}\).

blocks.prompt:

Give the value of x correct to 3 decimal places.
blocks.hint: Take logs of both sides and bring the exponent down.
blocks.solution:

Collect the terms to get \(x=\frac{\ln 27-\ln 7}{3\ln 7}\). Round at the end.

sections.title: When is an expression a disguised quadratic?
sections.label: Substitute
sections.intro: When one exponential term is the square of another, replace the smaller one with a positive variable. Solve the quadratic, then convert back.

blocks.html: With \(u=a^x\), the expression \(a^{2x}\) becomes \(u^2\) and \(u>0\).

blocks.prompt:

blocks.hint: Substitute a single positive variable for the basic exponential.

The quadratic factors as \((u-16)(u-64)=0\).

Both u-values are positive. Match the exponent \(x+3\) to \(2\) and \(3\) in turn.

\(x=-1\text{ or }x=0\)

retry.feedback: These are the values of the substituted variable. Convert them back to powers to find x.

blocks.html: A negative or zero value of the substituted variable cannot be an exponential value.

blocks.prompt: Find both exact solutions of \(2^{2x}-10\cdot 2^x+16=0\).
blocks.hint: Use \(u=2^x\) and factorise the quadratic in \(u\).

Setting \(u=2^x\) makes \(2^{2x}\) equal to \(u^2\). This gives \(u^2-10u+16=0\).

Factorise: \((u-2)(u-8)=0\). This gives the two positive candidates \(u=2\) and \(u=8\).

Solve the original power equation for each separately. The answers are \(x=1\) and \(x=3\).

blocks.html: For each positive solution in u, solve a separate exponential equation for x.

examples.title: Rewrite both sides before equating
examples.question: Solve \(8^{x+1}=4^{2x}\) exactly.
solution: Because \(8=2^3\) and \(4=2^2\), the equation becomes \(2^{3(x+1)}=2^{4x}\).
The base \(2\) is the same and distinct from \(1\), so \(3x+3=4x\).
Hence \(x=3\). Both original sides then equal \(2^{12}\).

examples.title: Convert a reciprocal base into a negative exponent
examples.question: Solve \(\left(\frac13\right)^{2x-1}=9^x\).
solution: Write the bases as \(3^{-1}\) and \(3^2\). The equation becomes \(3^{-(2x-1)}=3^{2x}\).
The entire left exponent is multiplied by \(-1\). Hence \(-2x+1=2x\) and \(x=\frac14\).
At this value both sides equal \(\sqrt3\).

examples.title: Isolate the power before taking logs
examples.question: Solve \(3\cdot2^x+1=16\). Give the exact answer and its value to three decimal places.
solution: Subtract \(1\) and divide by \(3\), giving \(2^x=5\). These are positive values, so logs can be taken.
Apply the power law after taking natural logs: \(x\ln 2=\ln 5\). Divide by \(\ln 2\).
\(x=\frac{\ln 5}{\ln 2}\approx2.322\). Keep the exact ratio until the final rounding step.

examples.title: Solve when both bases have a variable power
examples.question: Solve \(2^{x+1}=3^{x-1}\) exactly.
solution: Taking natural logs gives \((x+1)\ln 2=(x-1)\ln 3\).
Expand both sides and collect the \(x\)-terms: \(x(\ln 3-\ln 2)=\ln 2+\ln 3\).
The denominator is \(\ln(3/2)>0\), so \(x=\frac{\ln 6}{\ln(3/2)}\).

examples.title: Solve a quadratic in a power of two
examples.question: Solve \(2^{2x}-6\cdot2^x+8=0\).
solution: Let \(u=2^x\). This is positive and \(2^{2x}=u^2\), so the equation is \(u^2-6u+8=0\).
Factorise as \((u-2)(u-4)=0\), giving two positive values of \(u\).

examples.title: Reject a negative auxiliary root
examples.question: Solve \(3^{2x}+2\cdot3^x-3=0\).
solution: Let \(u=3^x>0\). Substitute to get \(u^2+2u-3=(u+3)(u-1)=0\).
The candidate \(u=-3\) cannot equal \(3^x\) for any real \(x\). The remaining candidate is \(u=1\).

examples.title: Cancel the natural logarithm and the exponential
examples.question: Simplify \(\ln(e^{\,2x-3})\) and solve \(\ln(e^{\,2x-3})=5\).
solution: For every real \(u\), \(\ln(e^u)=u\). Here \(u=2x-3\), so the simplified expression is \(2x-3\).
The original argument at this value is \(e^5>0\).

examples.title: Apply the inverse identity to an expression
examples.question: Solve \(e^{\ln(3-x)}=5\), stating the domain of the left side.
solution: The logarithm inside the exponential needs \(3-x>0\), so \(x<3\).
On this domain, \(e^{\ln(3-x)}=3-x\). Thus \(3-x=5\), giving \(x=-2\).
\(-2\) is in the original domain and \(e^{\ln 5}=5\).

examples.title: Keep the log of a constant as a separate term
examples.question: Simplify \(\ln(4e^{3x})\), then solve \(\ln(4e^{3x})=\ln 4+6\).
solution: The factors \(4\) and \(e^{3x}\) are both positive. Apply the product law: \(\ln(4e^{3x})=\ln 4+\ln(e^{3x})=\ln 4+3x\).
Subtract \(\ln 4\) from the two equal sides. Now \(3x=6\) and \(x=2\).
The logarithmic constant cancels only because it appears on both sides.

examples.title: Subtract two logs with a common factor
examples.question: Simplify \(\ln(6e^{x})-\ln(2e^{3x})\), then solve when its value is \(\ln 3+4\).
solution: Both arguments are positive for every real \(x\). Combining them gives \(\ln\!\left(\frac{6e^x}{2e^{3x}}\right)=\ln(3e^{-2x})\).
The product rule now gives \(\ln 3-2x\). Set this equal to \(\ln 3+4\).

examples.title: Recover both coordinates after a log substitution
examples.question: For \(x>0\), find the intersections of \(y=2\ln x\) and \(y=(\ln x)^2-3\).
solution: At an intersection the \(y\)-values agree. Put \(t=\ln x\), so \(2t=t^2-3\).
Then \(t^2-2t-3=(t-3)(t+1)=0\), giving \(t=3\) or \(t=-1\). Both are valid because \(\ln x\) can be any real number.
Recover \(x=e^t\) and substitute into \(y=2t\). The points are \((e^3,6)\) and \((e^{-1},-2)\).

examples.title: Recognise one intersection from a repeated root
examples.question: For \(x>0\), find the only intersection of \(y=4\ln x-4\) and \(y=(\ln x)^2\).
solution: Put \(t=\ln x\) and equate the two \(y\)-values: \(4t-4=t^2\).
Rearrange to \(t^2-4t+4=(t-2)^2=0\). This gives the single value \(t=2\).
\(x=e^2\) and \(y=t^2=4\), so the curves meet at \((e^2,4)\).

sections.title: How can I find a multiplier from two observations?

sections.intro: In a multiplicative model the same positive factor applies over equal time intervals. Divide the later observation by the earlier one to cancel the scale.

blocks.html: For \(P(t)=Ab^t\), the ratio over \(\Delta t\) time units is \(b^{\Delta t}\). The positive root recovers b.

blocks.prompt: A sensor reading follows \(R(t)=Ab^t\), with \(A,b>0\). The readings are \(R(1)=20\) and \(R(3)=45\). Find the exact multiplier \(b\).
blocks.hint: Divide the later reading by the earlier one to cancel the initial scale.
blocks.solution:
Divide the model values at \(t=3\) and \(t=1\): \(b^{3-1}=\frac{9}{4}\).

There are 2 time units between the readings. The positive root gives \(b=\frac{3}{2}\).

blocks.html: The ratio of observations may describe several intervals. It is not automatically the one-step factor.

blocks.prompt: A sensor reading follows \(R(t)=Ab^t\), with \(A,b>0\). The readings are \(R(3)=40\) and \(R(5)=10\). Find the exact multiplier \(b\).
blocks.hint: Divide the later reading by the earlier one to cancel the initial scale.
blocks.solution:
Divide the model values at \(t=5\) and \(t=3\): \(b^{5-3}=\frac{1}{4}\).

There are 2 time units between the readings. The positive root gives \(b=\frac{1}{2}\).

sections.title: When does a decaying measurement reach a known level?
sections.label: Threshold
sections.intro: Find the time at which the reading equals its target. Isolate the exponential first. If the model approaches a non-zero background level, subtract that level before dividing.

blocks.html: For \(R=Ae^{-kt}\) with \(A,k>0\), set \(R=L\). Then \(e^{-kt}=\dfrac{L}{A}\), so \(t=\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{A}{L}\right)}{k}\). A target can be reached at \(t\geq0\) only when \(0<L\leq A\). For \(R=B+Ae^{-kt}\), apply the same method to the amount above \(B\), which is \(L-B\) at the target.

figure.alt: Decreasing exponential model crossing a horizontal alert line once.
figure.caption: Read from the threshold to the curve, then down to time. The logarithm gives the crossing without measuring the sketch.

blocks.prompt:
A sensor records \(R=22e^{-\frac{1}{5}t}\) for time t in hours. The alert level is \(\frac{11}{2}\).

Find the time at which the reading reaches the alert level. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
blocks.hint: Isolate the exponential factor and use the natural logarithm.
blocks.solution:
Divide by \(22\). This gives \(e^{-\frac{1}{5}t}=\frac{1}{4}\).

Take logs and divide by the negative coefficient of t, obtaining \(t=\frac{-\ln(\frac{1}{4})}{\frac{1}{5}}\).

\(6.931\text{ h}\)

blocks.prompt: A signal has strength \(R=32e^{-\frac{t}{5}}\) after \(t\) hours. When does its strength become \(12\) units? Give your answer in hours to 3 decimal places.
blocks.hint: Set \(R=12\), divide by the starting strength, and take natural logarithms.
blocks.solution: \[e^{-\frac{t}{5}}=\frac{12}{32}=\frac{3}{8}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad t=5\ln\frac{8}{3}\approx4.904\text{ hours}.\]

blocks.html: In a decay model with a background level \(B\), the quantity \(R-B\) decays. Taking the logarithm before you isolate that quantity can select the wrong time.

blocks.prompt: An indicator reads \(R=30e^{-t/4}\) units after \(t\) hours. At what time does the reading reach \(10\) units? Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
blocks.hint: Write the target as a fraction of the initial reading before taking logs.
blocks.solution:
Divide by \(30\) to get \(e^{-t/4}=\frac13\). Take logs on both sides.

Then \(-\frac{t}4=\ln(1/3)=-\ln3\), so \(t=4\ln3\approx4.394\) hours.

retry.feedback: The model decreases after the initial reading. Remember the minus sign on the coefficient of time.

blocks.prompt: After \(t\) minutes, a sensor reads \(R=18+40e^{-\frac{t}{6}}\). When is the reading \(28\)? Give your answer in minutes to 3 decimal places.
blocks.hint: Find how far the target reading is above the background reading of \(18\).
blocks.solution:
Subtract \(18\) to get \(40e^{-\frac{t}{6}}=10\).

\[e^{-\frac{t}{6}}=\frac{1}{4}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad t=6\ln 4\approx8.318\text{ minutes}.\]

blocks.html:
Leave your calculator result unrounded until the final step. Use the model's time unit and check that the target lies in the range for \(t\geq0\).

In Extra practice, compare a quantity that falls and one that rises by a fixed factor.

sections.title: What does the model say before the reference reading?
sections.label: Interpret
sections.intro: A negative time means earlier than the chosen reference. It does not mean a negative measurement.

blocks.html: For \(P(t)=Ab^t\), the reference reading is \(P(0)=A\) and the reading one interval earlier is \(P(-1)=\frac{A}{b}\).

blocks.prompt:
A reading obeys \(R(t)=A\,b^t\). At the reference time \(t=0\), it is \(21\). Over the next \(6\) intervals it becomes \(21\).

Find the exact value of \(b\).
blocks.hint: Use the ratio of the later and initial readings to find b.
blocks.solution:
The reference reading gives \(A=21\).

Divide the later reading by the reference reading and take the positive \(6\)th root.

\(1\)

blocks.html: A model prediction outside the measured interval is an extrapolation.

blocks.prompt: A reading follows \(R(t)=Ab^t\), with \(b>0\). It is \(60\) at the reference time \(t=0\) and \(120\) one hour before. Find \(b\).
blocks.hint: One hour before the reference time corresponds to a negative exponent.

retry.feedback: The reading doubles when going backwards. The requested multiplier is for going forwards.

blocks.html: Distinguish the reference time from the first time the process really existed.

examples.title: Recover a multiplier from two readings
examples.question: A culture grows by a fixed factor per hour. A model \(G(t)=Ab^t\) gives \(G(1)=24\) and \(G(3)=54\). Find \(b\) and \(A\).
solution: The observations give \(Ab=24\) and \(Ab^3=54\). Divide the second by the first: \(b^2=\frac{54}{24}=\frac94\). The gap is two hours.
The multiplier is positive, so \(b=\frac32\). From the first reading, \(A=\frac{24}{3/2}=16\).
Check both observations: \(16\cdot\frac32=24\) and \(16\cdot\frac{27}{8}=54\).

examples.title: Recover a model with a fractional multiplier
examples.question: A filter has readings \(R(2)=32\) and \(R(5)=4\), where \(R(t)=Ab^t\). Find \(b\) and \(A\).
solution: The later reading is smaller, so expect \(0<b<1\). Divide over the three-unit gap: \(b^{5-2}=\frac4{32}=\frac18\).
Take the positive cube root to obtain \(b=\frac12\). Since \(32=A\left(\frac12\right)^2\), \(A=128\).
The model predicts \(128\left(\frac12\right)^5=4\), as required.

examples.title: Find the time at which a reading reaches its target
examples.question:
A signal has strength \(R=60e^{-\frac{t}{4}}\) after \(t\) hours, where \(t\geq0\).

  1. Find when the signal reaches \(25\) units. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

    [3]

  2. Explain why it reaches this strength exactly once.

    [1]
solution: (a) Set \(60e^{-\frac{t}{4}}=25\). Dividing by \(60\) gives \(e^{-\frac{t}{4}}=\dfrac{5}{12}\).
\[-\frac{t}{4}=\ln\frac{5}{12}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad t=4\ln\frac{12}{5}\approx3.502\text{ hours}.\]
(b) The strength decreases strictly from \(60\) towards \(0\), passing \(25\) once.

examples.title: Take the temperature above room level first
examples.question:
A mug of tea has temperature \(T=20+60e^{-\frac{3t}{10}}\) °C after \(t\geq0\) minutes.

  1. Find when the tea first reaches \(50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\). Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

    [3]

  2. According to this model, does it reach exactly \(20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) in a finite time? Explain your answer.

    [1]
solution: (a) The temperature is \(30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) above room level at the target. Subtract \(20\) from \(50\), then divide by \(60\), giving \(e^{-\frac{3t}{10}}=\dfrac{1}{2}\).
\[t=\frac{10}{3}\ln 2\approx2.310\text{ minutes}.\]
(b) For finite \(t\), \(e^{-\frac{3t}{10}}>0\). The temperature stays above \(20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and approaches it as time increases.

examples.title: Work back to before the reference time
examples.question: A reading obeys \(R(t)=80\left(\frac12\right)^t\), where \(t\) counts weeks from a service date. Find the model readings one week before and two weeks after that date.
solution: One week before the service date is \(t=-1\). Since \(\left(\frac12\right)^{-1}=2\), the model gives \(R(-1)=160\).
Two weeks afterwards is \(t=2\). The reading is halved twice: \(R(2)=80\left(\frac12\right)^2=20\).
The negative input represents an earlier time. The reading itself remains positive.

examples.title: Tell the rate from the multiplier
examples.question: A forecast uses \(N(t)=64\left(\frac54\right)^t\) in weeks. Find the percentage increase per week and the forecast change from week 0 to week 2.
solution: Over one week the factor is \(\frac54=1.25\), meaning an increase of \(25\%\).
Over two weeks use the factor twice: \(N(2)=64\left(\frac54\right)^2=64\cdot\frac{25}{16}=100\).
The change from \(64\) to \(100\) is \(36\). The overall factor is \(\frac{25}{16}=1.5625\), an increase of \(56.25\%\).

extraPractice.prompt: A detector reads \(S=12+45e^{-t/2}\), where \(t\) is in hours. When does \(S\) reach \(21\)? Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

Take logs to obtain \(-\frac{t}2=\ln(1/5)=-\ln5\). Thus \(t=2\ln5\approx3.219\) hours.

extraPractice.prompt: After \(t\) hours a model predicts \(N=24\left(\frac32\right)^t\). When does it reach \(72\)? Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
extraPractice.hint: Isolate the power, then use the power law to bring its exponent in front of the logarithm.
extraPractice.solution:
Divide by \(24\) to get \(\left(\frac32\right)^t=3\). Taking logs gives \(t\ln(3/2)=\ln3\).

Divide by \(\ln(3/2)\) and round the result. The time is \(2.710\) hours.

extraPractice.prompt: A reading obeys \(R(t)=50\left(\frac58\right)^t\). Find \(R(-1)\).
extraPractice.hint: Use the reciprocal of \(\frac58\) for the interval before the reference time.
extraPractice.solution: \(R(-1)=50\left(\frac58\right)^{-1}=50\cdot\frac85=80\). The reading was higher before the decay.

extraPractice.prompt: A model predicts \(R(t)=A\left(\frac32\right)^t\). Find the exact ratio of the reading one interval after the reference time to the reading one interval before it.
extraPractice.hint: The observations are at \(t=1\) and \(t=-1\). There are two intervals between them.

revision.body:
How can I find a multiplier from two observations?

For \(P(t)=Ab^t\), the ratio over \(\Delta t\) time units is \(b^{\Delta t}\). The positive root recovers b.

When does a decaying measurement reach a known level?

For positive \(A,k,L\), \(Ae^{-kt}=L\) gives \(t=\frac{\ln(A/L)}{k}\) and represents non-negative time when \(L\le A\).

What does the model say before the reference reading?

For \(P(t)=Ab^t\), the reference reading is \(P(0)=A\) and the reading one interval earlier is \(P(-1)=\frac{A}{b}\).

addmaths-0606-logs-exp-graphs.description: Find intercepts, asymptotes, range and direction for y = k eⁿˣ + a.

sections.title: Where does a shifted exponential level out?
sections.label: Asymptote
sections.intro: Follow the direction in which the exponential term tends to zero. That is where the graph approaches its asymptote.

blocks.html: For \(y=ke^{nx}+a\) with \(kn\ne0\), the asymptote is \(y=a\). The y-intercept is \((0,k+a)\).

figure.alt: An increasing exponential curve lying above a horizontal dashed line.
figure.caption: The horizontal asymptote is \(y=2\). The point at \(x=0\) is one unit higher.

blocks.prompt:
The curve has equation \(y=-5e^{x}+5\).

State the equation of its horizontal asymptote.
blocks.hint: Find the limiting y-value when the exponential term tends to zero.
blocks.solution:
The exponential term tends to zero as x tends to negative infinity.

The remaining vertical shift is \(5\).

\(y=5\)

retry.feedback: That is the y-intercept. The asymptote is the limit when the exponential term tends to zero.

blocks.html: The graph generally crosses the vertical axis at a different height from its horizontal asymptote.

blocks.prompt: State the equation of the horizontal asymptote of \(y=3e^{-x}-2\).
blocks.hint: Decide whether the exponential term tends to zero as x moves to the left or the right.
blocks.solution: As \(x\) tends to positive infinity, \(e^{-x}\) tends to zero. The remaining constant gives the asymptote \(y=-2\).

retry.feedback: This is the height when \(x=0\). The horizontal asymptote is the limiting height.

blocks.html: Mark the asymptote with a dashed line and draw the curve on the correct side.

sections.title: Can a shifted exponential cross the x-axis?
sections.label: Axis crossing
sections.intro: Set the whole curve equal to zero. A crossing only exists when isolating the exponential term gives a strictly positive number.

blocks.html: For \(y=ke^{nx}+a\), a crossing requires \(-a/k>0\). Taking logs then gives its exact x-coordinate.

blocks.prompt:
Consider \(y=8e^{4x}-11\).

Find the x-coordinate of the intercept. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
blocks.hint: Set y to zero and isolate the exponential before taking logs.
blocks.solution:
On the x-axis, y is zero. Isolate the exponential to get \(e^{4x}=\frac{11}{8}\).

The exact coordinate is \(\frac{\ln(\frac{11}{8})}{4}\). Round only at the end.

\(x\approx 0.080\)

blocks.html: The exponent at a crossing need not be zero. First move the vertical translation.

blocks.prompt:
Consider \(y=3e^{4x}-12\).

Find the x-coordinate of the intercept. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
blocks.hint: Set y to zero and isolate the exponential before taking logs.
blocks.solution:
On the x-axis, y is zero. Isolate the exponential to get \(e^{4x}=4\).

The exact coordinate is \(\frac{\ln(4)}{4}\). Round only at the end.

\(x\approx 0.347\)

blocks.html: Check the side of the asymptote before searching for a crossing.

sections.title: How do the graph features recover the parameters?
sections.label: Parameters
sections.intro: Read the vertical shift from the horizontal asymptote. Subtract the shift from the y-intercept to recover the scale.

blocks.html: At \(x=0\), the exponential is \(e^0=1\). The intercept is the sum of the scale and the shift.

Find the value of k.
blocks.hint: Read the translation from the asymptote, then substitute x = 0.
blocks.solution:
The asymptote gives \(a=10\).

At the y-intercept the exponential is 1. Subtract \(10\) from the intercept.

\(4\)

examples.title: Read a curve that lies below its asymptote
examples.question: For \(y=5-4e^x\), state the horizontal asymptote, the \(y\)-intercept, and the range. Describe the shape you would sketch.
solution: As \(x\) tends to negative infinity, \(e^x\) tends to zero. The horizontal asymptote is \(y=5\). Because \(4e^x>0\), every point lies below it.
At \(x=0\), the value is \(5-4e^0=1\), so the \(y\)-intercept is \((0,1)\). The range is \(y<5\).
\(e^x\) increases with \(x\), so subtracting \(4e^x\) makes the curve decrease. Start just below the dashed line at the left and pass through \((0,1)\).

examples.title: Identify the direction of approach
examples.question: For \(y=2e^{-x}-3\), state the asymptote, the \(y\)-intercept and the range.
solution: As \(x\) increases, \(-x\) decreases. The term \(2e^{-x}\) tends to zero towards the right, so \(y=-3\) is the horizontal asymptote.
At \(x=0\), \(y=2(1)-3=-1\), giving \((0,-1)\). The exponential factor is positive, so the whole curve is above \(y=-3\).
The curve decreases from arbitrarily large values and approaches \(-3\) from above. Its range is \(y>-3\).

examples.title: Locate the crossing and explain uniqueness
examples.question: Find the exact \(x\)-intercept of \(y=3e^{2x}-6\). Explain why there is only one crossing.
solution: At a crossing \(y=0\), so \(3e^{2x}=6\) and \(e^{2x}=2\).
Taking natural logs gives \(2x=\ln 2\). The point is \(\left(\frac{\ln2}{2},0\right)\).
The function \(e^{2x}\) is strictly increasing, so it takes the value \(2\) at most once.

examples.title: Explain when a crossing is impossible
examples.question: Does \(y=2e^{3x}+4\) have an \(x\)-intercept? State the condition on \(c\) for the line \(y=c\) to meet the curve.
solution: Every output is strictly above \(4\), since \(2e^{3x}>0\). Therefore the line \(y=0\) cannot meet it.
Setting \(2e^{3x}+4=c\) gives \(e^{3x}=\frac{c-4}{2}\). This has a real solution precisely when the right side is positive.
There is one intersection if \(c>4\). At \(c=4\) the line is the asymptote.

examples.title: Use the intercept to recover the vertical scale
examples.question: The curve \(y=ke^{2x}+a\) passes through \((0,13)\) and has asymptote \(y=10\). Find \(a\), \(k\), and the exact value of \(y\) at \(x=\frac12\).
solution: The asymptote gives \(a=10\). At the intercept \(e^0=1\), so \(k+10=13\), giving \(k=3\).
At \(x=\frac12\) the exponent is \(2\cdot\frac12=1\). The output is \(3e+10\).

examples.title: Use two graph features to recover a negative scale
examples.question: The graph \(y=ke^{-x}+a\) has asymptote \(y=3\) and crosses the \(x\)-axis at \(x=\ln 2\). Find \(k\) and the \(y\)-intercept.
solution: Read \(a=3\) from the asymptote. At the crossing, \(0=ke^{-\ln2}+3=\frac{k}{2}+3\).
The negative scale puts the whole curve below the asymptote, consistent with both intercepts.

examples.title: Distinguish the asymptote from the crossing
examples.question: For \(y=2\ln(3-x)\), find the natural domain, vertical asymptote and \(x\)-intercept.
solution: The argument is positive when \(3-x>0\), or \(x<3\). The boundary where the argument tends to zero is \(x=3\), the vertical asymptote.
At an \(x\)-intercept \(y=0\), so \(\ln(3-x)=0\). The argument is then \(1\), giving \(3-x=1\) and \(x=2\).
The point \((2,0)\) is on the permitted side \(x<3\).

examples.title: Read the graph on the right of the boundary
examples.question: For \(y=\ln(2x+4)\), find the domain and both intercepts.
solution: The positive argument condition is \(2x+4>0\), so \(x>-2\). Thus \(x=-2\) is the vertical asymptote.
For \(y=0\), the argument must equal \(1\): \(2x+4=1\) gives \(x=-\frac32\).
The value \(x=0\) is in the domain. The two intercepts are \(\left(-\frac32,0\right)\) and \((0,\ln4)\).

examples.title: Recover the shift from an asymptote
examples.question: The curve \(y=2\ln(3x+b)\) has asymptote \(x=-1\). Find \(b\) and the exact intercepts.
solution: The argument tends to zero at the asymptote. Solve \(3(-1)+b=0\), giving \(b=3\). The domain is \(x>-1\).
For \(y=0\), solve \(3x+3=1\), giving \(x=-\frac23\).
\(x=0\) is allowed and the output there is \(2\ln3\). The intercepts are \(\left(-\frac23,0\right)\) and \((0,2\ln3)\).

examples.title: Use the intercept to locate the asymptote
examples.question: The graph \(y=\ln(2x+b)\) crosses the \(x\)-axis at \(x=2\). Find \(b\) and explain whether there is a \(y\)-intercept.
solution: For the output to be zero, the argument must be one. Thus \(2(2)+b=1\), giving \(b=-3\).
The domain is \(2x-3>0\), or \(x>\frac32\). The boundary \(x=\frac32\) is the vertical asymptote.
The \(y\)-axis has \(x=0\), outside the domain, so there is no \(y\)-intercept.

examples.title: Track two reflections
examples.question: State the domain and direction of \(y=-2\ln(4-x)\). Find its \(x\)-intercept.
solution: The domain is \(x<4\), found from \(4-x>0\). The asymptote is \(x=4\).
As \(x\) increases, \(4-x\) gets smaller and its logarithm decreases. Multiplication by \(-2\) reverses that change, so \(y\) increases.
At \(y=0\), the log argument is \(1\). Thus \(4-x=1\), giving \((3,0)\).

examples.title: Track the direction on the valid side
examples.question: Describe the monotonicity of \(y=-\ln(x+1)\). State the asymptote and the side on which the graph lies.
solution: The domain is \(x>-1\). The asymptote is \(x=-1\), and the curve is on its right.
\(x+1\) grows as \(x\) grows, so \(\ln(x+1)\) increases. Its negative therefore decreases.
Close to the asymptote, the argument tends to \(0\) from above, so \(\ln(x+1)\) tends to negative infinity and \(y\) tends to positive infinity.

sections.title: How do I invert a shifted exponential?
sections.label: Undo exponential
sections.intro: Name the output y, remove any translation and scale, take the logarithm and divide by the coefficient of x. Then use x as the inverse input.

blocks.html: Inverting \(y=ke^{nx}+a\) uses \(x=\frac1n\ln\left(\frac{y-a}{k}\right)\). The quotient inside ln must be positive.

blocks.prompt:
The function \(f(x)=3e^{7x}+7\) is defined for all real x.

Find \(f^{-1}(x)\).
blocks.hint: Isolate the original exponential before taking logs.
blocks.solution:
Let y be the original output. Isolate the exponential as \(e^{7x}=\frac{y-7}{3}\).

Take natural logs and divide by \(7\). Write the original output as the variable of the inverse.

\(f^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{7}\ln\left(\frac{x-7}{3}\right)\)

blocks.html: Subtract the shift and divide by the scale before applying the logarithm.

Add \(5\) and divide by \(6\) to isolate the original input.

examples.title: Undo a shift and scale in the right order
examples.question: Find the inverse of \(f(x)=2e^{3x}+1\) and give its domain.
solution: Set \(y=2e^{3x}+1\). Subtract \(1\), then divide by \(2\): \(e^{3x}=\frac{y-1}{2}\).
Taking natural logs gives \(3x=\ln\!\left(\frac{y-1}{2}\right)\). Rename the input to obtain \(f^{-1}(x)=\frac13\ln\!\left(\frac{x-1}{2}\right)\).
The original range is \(y>1\), so the inverse has domain \(x>1\).

examples.title: Invert an exponential below its asymptote
examples.question: Find the inverse of \(f(x)=5-3e^x\) and explain its input restriction.
solution: From \(y=5-3e^x\), isolate the exponential: \(3e^x=5-y\), so \(e^x=\frac{5-y}{3}\).
For \(x=\ln\!\left(\frac{5-y}{3}\right)\) to exist, the argument must be positive, which requires \(y<5\).
Thus \(f^{-1}(x)=\ln\!\left(\frac{5-x}{3}\right)\) for \(x<5\). The original range is below the horizontal asymptote.

examples.title: Undo a logarithm with a multiplier
examples.question: Find the inverse of \(h(x)=2\ln(3x-6)\) and state its domain and range.
solution: The original domain is \(x>2\). With \(y=2\ln(3x-6)\), divide by \(2\) and exponentiate: \(e^{y/2}=3x-6\).
Adding \(6\) and dividing by \(3\) gives \(h^{-1}(x)=\frac{e^{x/2}+6}{3}\).
The original logarithm has all real outputs, so every real number is an inverse input. The inverse outputs satisfy \(y>2\).

examples.title: Invert a logarithm with a decreasing argument
examples.question: Find the inverse of \(h(x)=\ln(4-2x)\) and state its range.
solution: The original domain is \(4-2x>0\), or \(x<2\). Every real output is possible because the argument reaches every positive value.
From \(y=\ln(4-2x)\), exponentiate to get \(e^y=4-2x\). Rearrange to \(2x=4-e^y\).
The inverse is \(h^{-1}(x)=\frac{4-e^x}{2}\), with range \(y<2\), since \(e^x>0\).

examples.title: Find one inverse value without a whole rule
examples.question: Let \(f(x)=\log_3(2x+1)\) on its natural domain. Find \(f^{-1}(2)\).
solution: An inverse output is an original input. Solve \(f(u)=2\) for that input \(u\).
The argument at \(4\) is \(9\), so the input is valid and \(f^{-1}(2)=4\).

examples.title: Test whether the inverse value exists
examples.question: Let \(g(x)=3+2e^x\). Find \(g^{-1}(9)\) and explain whether \(g^{-1}(3)\) exists.
solution: Thus \(g^{-1}(9)=\ln3\). An original output of \(3\) would require \(e^u=0\).
The exponential is strictly positive, so \(3\) is outside the inverse domain and \(g^{-1}(3)\) is undefined.
